name: traits
intent: Attach behaviour, associated types and constants to a type from the outside, in a separate specialisable descriptor, so that generic code selects the right implementation from a type's properties instead of from an interface the type must inherit.
problem: A generic algorithm has to adapt to the properties of the types it is instantiated with - is this type numeric, does it expose a nested value_type, how does it compare, what is its end-of-sequence value, is it trivially copyable? The types carrying those properties are built-in or third-party types that cannot be edited to declare them, and forcing them behind a common base class is intrusive, costs runtime dispatch and cannot be applied to fundamental types at all.
context: Generic (templated or compile-time-generic) libraries and algorithms that must work over types they do not own: containers and iterators, numeric and character utilities, serialisation, formatting, hashing and comparison frameworks, capability-dependent fast paths. Applies when the type's properties are knowable before the program runs and the design is free to describe the type from outside - and, with the same intent, wherever languages express ad-hoc polymorphism through type classes, implicit evidence, constraints or protocol conformance.
benefits: Non-intrusive: a type's properties can be described, corrected or extended from the outside without editing the type - which is the only way to describe built-in and third-party types at all.

One indirection point: algorithms depend on the trait interface instead of the members of each concrete type, so the algorithm is written once and a new type joins it by supplying a description (retroactive modelling).
No runtime cost where the trait is resolved at compile time: static dispatch, no vtable, no allocation, and operations that inline.
Enables optimisations a generic body otherwise cannot express - dispatch on iterator category, a memcpy fast path for trivially copyable types, per-type precision, radix and end-of-file constants.
Replaces inheritance as a categorisation mechanism: types that cannot or should not share a base class (fundamentals, third-party classes, array types) still participate in the generic algorithm.

Keeps type knowledge in one documented place per type instead of scattered type tests, and lets a user substitute an alternative interpretation (a case-insensitive char_traits) without touching the algorithm.
tradeoffs: One specialization per type (or per family): a trait that must be specialized for many classes in a hierarchy produces a long tail of boilerplate, and a whole-hierarchy technique is needed to avoid it.

A trait's members are not checked for meaning: the compiler verifies that a specialization is well-formed, not that it returns the right answer, so a wrong but plausible description silently misbehaves.

Diagnostics are hostile: failures surface deep inside library internals (substitution failures, missing nested members, 'no matching function') unless the language has a direct way to state the requirement.

Purely static: the choice is fixed before the program runs; varying it at runtime needs the description to become a value (a runtime traits object, a strategy object, type erasure), which reintroduces the indirection the pattern was meant to avoid.

Trait proliferation: many near-empty one-member descriptors enlarge the API surface and the build, while the opposite - one traits blob - forces a user who needs a single member changed to reimplement all of them.

Extensibility is one-directional and unchecked: an unsupported type can be described incorrectly and fails only at the point of use, and where a language forbids external implementations (orphan rules) the non-intrusive promise does not hold at all.

participants.responsibility: A template or type that aggregates, for one type or family of types, the associated types, constants and operations the generic algorithm needs; it holds no state and adds no size to anything.
Written only against the descriptor's interface, instantiated for any type for which the descriptor yields the required items, and never against the concrete type's own members.

The built-in, third-party or user type whose properties are needed; it may satisfy the descriptor intrinsically (through nested members) or only through a binding written elsewhere, and it stays unmodified.
Supplies the fallback description for types that already expose the required members, or deliberately fails to compile for types nobody described.

The per-type binding - partial or full specialization, implicit instance, conformance, type token - that fills the descriptor's interface for a type that cannot or should not expose the members itself.

use_cases: Iterator and range libraries that need value_type, reference, difference_type and an iterator category from every iterator - including raw pointers, for which no nested member can exist.
Numeric and character/string utilities that need per-type limits, precision and constants (numeric_limits) or a type's end-of-file value and comparison rules (char_traits).
Formatting, serialisation, hashing and comparison frameworks that must support types from other libraries by describing them from the outside (formatters, codecs, hash functions, ordering instances).

Capability-dependent implementations: detect whether a type has push_back/begin/serialize and pick the efficient or the safe implementation (memcpy fast path for trivially copyable types, buffered vs unbuffered readers).

Cross-language ad-hoc polymorphism: type classes, implicit evidence, generic constraints or protocol conformance give behaviour to types you do not own without subclassing them (Ordering, INumber<T>, Numeric, deserialiser registries).
Unit, quantity and domain-type libraries carrying per-type properties (dimension, epsilon, radix, zero/one identity) that the generic arithmetic code must consult.

{fmt} formatting of user-defined types: a formatter<T> specialization or a format_as conversion written beside the type joins it to fmt's formatting algorithm, which then handles types it was never compiled against.

serde (de)serialising structs from other crates through Serialize/Deserialize bindings written outside the data type - a remote-derive definition or newtype wrapper - because Rust's orphan rules forbid attaching the impl to a foreign type directly.

Haskell type classes binding operations (equality, show, arithmetic overloading) to types like Int or Maybe through instances declared apart from the type, and Swift protocol extensions retroactively conforming system types such as Date to Identifiable.
avoid_when: You control the types and a common interface is natural: plain virtual dispatch or an ordinary interface is simpler and additionally supports runtime substitution.
There is exactly one type in play: the descriptor indirection buys nothing, so write the code directly.
The decision is genuinely runtime state (configuration, tenant, feature flag) rather than a property of the type: use a registry or configuration lookup instead (Feature Toggle).
You need heterogeneous values behind one runtime type: use an interface or type erasure; a trait cannot give runtime polymorphism.

The language already expresses the requirement directly (concepts and requires-clauses, generic constraints and type sets, type-class instances, structural protocols, reified generics with typeof): state the constraint there and keep a descriptor only for the associated payload.
anti_patterns: Traits blob: stuffing unrelated properties into one descriptor, so a user who must change one member has to reimplement all of them.
Static re-implementation of polymorphism: using traits (or SFINAE detection) where a virtual interface or a plain overload would be clearer, then losing runtime substitutability for no measured gain.

Assuming a binding is correct because it compiles - no documented contract, no requirement check, no compile-time assertion on the descriptor's own members (see P2279 for the standardised form of this complaint).
A confidently guessing default mapping: deducing an element type, size or behaviour for types nobody described instead of failing at the point of description.
Specialising a descriptor where the algorithm cannot find it - another namespace, a different template, a later point of instantiation - so the description exists but is silently invisible.
design_principles: Program to an interface, not an implementation: the generic code names the descriptor and never the concrete type's members.
Open/closed: new types join an existing algorithm through a description supplied elsewhere, without modifying the algorithm or the type.
Extra level of indirection: the descriptor is the seam that decouples what the algorithm needs from what the type provides.
Non-intrusive extension: prefer describing a type from the outside over editing it or forcing it into an inheritance hierarchy.
One concept per (meta)function: single-responsibility descriptors, named after the property they describe, keep bindings small and contracts checkable.
best_practices: Prefer several small descriptors, each named after the property it describes, over one blob: a binding then touches only what actually differs.

Write the property's contract down and check the required members (named requirement, concept, static_assert, compile-time probe) so a wrong binding fails at the binding instead of deep inside the algorithm.
Provide a useful default mapping for types that already carry the members and specialise only for types that cannot be edited; document which types are supported.

Re-export the descriptor into the described type as a nested member (traits_type, Item, Element) and spell dependent member types with the language's disambiguation keyword, so generic code and diagnostics stay readable.
Keep the descriptor stateless and its members constant/static - it costs neither size nor runtime; pass a descriptor as an object only when the property must vary at runtime.

Prefer the language's direct constraint mechanism where it exists (concepts, requires-clauses, generic constraints, type-class instances) and keep the descriptor for the associated items a constraint cannot carry.
sources: Nathan C. Myers, 'Traits: a new and useful template technique', C++ Report, June 1995 - the article that named the idiom and defined a traits class as 'a class used in place of template parameters'.
Philip Wadler and Stephen Blott, 'How to make ad-hoc polymorphism less ad hoc', POPL 1989 - the origin of type classes, the instance/implicit-evidence family this pattern generalises.
